name: LangGraph multi-agent routing (supervisor pattern)
decomposition_method: LLM-prompted (zero-shot/CoT). The supervisor LLM reads the incoming user message and, via tool-calling, decides which specialist agent to invoke. There is no separate decomposition module: any splitting of a compound prompt into sub-tasks is implicit in the supervisor's reasoning/handoff loop rather than an explicit decompose step. Optionally a handoff tool can carry a task_description argument the supervisor fills in, which acts as a lightweight per-handoff sub-task statement.
decomposition_granularity: tool call (one handoff per specialist agent invocation; the task_description field, when used, frames a sub-task as a milestone-like instruction).
ordering_strategy: dynamic (mid-chain re-plan). The supervisor re-evaluates after each worker returns and chooses the next agent (or FINISH). Effectively sequential per step but order is decided turn-by-turn, not committed upfront as a DAG.
decomposition_validation: None. There is no detector, reward model, or explicit check of solvability/completeness/non-redundancy of any decomposition. The system blindly trusts the supervisor LLM's routing choices. Quality control is limited to prompt engineering of the supervisor and the recursion_limit guard, which only catches non-termination (routing loops), not bad-but-terminating decompositions.
hierarchy_depth: multi-level tree. Supervisors can manage other supervisors (create_supervisor over teams), enabling nested delegation; a single supervisor over flat workers is the common two-level case.
router_type: single-label classifier per step (the supervisor emits exactly one handoff tool call per routing decision). Over multiple turns this composes into a chain. It is not a graph planner: no full DAG is produced upfront. [uncertain] Some LangChain chat models can emit parallel tool calls, which could trigger multiple handoffs in one turn, but the base supervisor pattern is documented as one-agent-at-a-time.
routing_model: prompted LLM (same class as main). Any LangChain-compatible chat model passed via model= acts as supervisor/router (examples use gpt-4o); model-agnostic. No separate fine-tuned classifier or embedding router.
handles_ambiguity: best-effort pick (overconfident-allow). No explicit ambiguity resolution, abstain, or clarification mechanism is built in; the supervisor LLM resolves ambiguity from its prompt and the handoff-tool descriptions. Clarification to the user is only possible if hand-coded into the supervisor prompt or via a human-in-the-loop interrupt, not provided by the pattern itself.
fallback_behavior: route to general LLM / error-abort. When no specialist clearly fits, behavior depends on the supervisor prompt: it may answer directly (acting as general LLM), keep routing (risking a loop), or terminate. There is no dedicated no-skill-covers fallback node; hitting recursion_limit raises an error. Re-decomposition is not automatic.
skill_pool_scale_and_retrieval: full-context (all agents in prompt). Every handoff tool definition (one per specialist) is placed in the supervisor's context, so scaling is bounded by the routing LLM's context window and degraded routing accuracy as the agent count grows. No built-in embedding retrieval, top-k filtering, or skill-tree traversal to shortlist agents; large pools must be managed by nesting supervisors (hierarchical sharding) rather than retrieval.
router_agent_asymmetry: Low / symmetric by default. The supervisor routes from handoff-tool names + descriptions, and the executing subagent receives the forwarded message history (full_history or last_message). There is no deliberate design giving the router richer skill text than the agent; both operate on the same descriptions. [uncertain]
execution_pattern: sequential chain. Supervisor picks one agent, waits for its result, then re-evaluates and routes again until FINISH. No documented native parallel fan-out of multiple subagents in the base pattern.
parallel_vs_concurrent: Neither by default; execution is sequential. [uncertain] Models that emit parallel tool calls could in principle issue multiple handoffs in one API turn, but true concurrent subagent execution is not a documented feature of langgraph-supervisor.
dependency_detection: assumed-sequential (default, conservative). Because the supervisor re-plans after every worker, dependencies are handled implicitly by ordering; there is no explicit independence analysis to enable safe parallelization.
result_aggregation: LLM joiner with configurable output_mode. Worker outputs return to the supervisor, which reads them and decides next action or composes the final answer. output_mode=full_history appends all worker messages to state; last_message surfaces only the worker's final reply. create_forward_message_tool lets the supervisor forward a worker's last message verbatim to output without paraphrasing/re-tokenizing.
mid_chain_feedback: hard (explicit re-planning). The supervisor node runs again after each worker, with prior results in state, so it can re-route, dispatch a different specialist, or finish based on intermediate outputs. This is the core control loop, not an add-on.
benchmark_name: None published with the library. No standardized benchmark (e.g., BFCL, ToolBench) is reported for the supervisor pattern itself; evaluation is left to the user (third-party guides describe building custom LangGraph multi-agent evals). [uncertain]
multi_intent_coverage: Not benchmarked. The pattern can in principle handle sequential (dependent) multi-intent prompts via iterative handoffs, but there is no benchmark categorizing parallel vs sequential vs mixed multi-intent coverage. [uncertain]
accuracy_metric: Not defined by the library; any accuracy measurement is user-supplied. In practice teams use outcome-only or state-based evaluation of the final multi-agent answer. [uncertain]
clarification_capability: Not measured and not built in. The pattern has no when-to-ask vs when-to-answer mechanism or clarification-efficiency metric; clarification must be hand-coded into the supervisor prompt or via human-in-the-loop interrupts. No ClarifyBench/InteractComp-style evaluation is provided.
process_vs_outcome_eval: outcome-oriented in practice; no built-in process supervision of intermediate routing steps. [uncertain]
eval_stability: Not applicable / not addressed. No bundled benchmark, so no claims about API-drift resistance or reproducibility; depends entirely on the user's eval harness. [uncertain]
integration_pattern: LangGraph node (pre-execute) / in-context. The supervisor is a StateGraph node (create_supervisor returns a compilable StateGraph); specialist agents are nodes or subgraphs reached via Command(goto=..., graph=Command.PARENT). Integrates as application-layer orchestration within a LangGraph app, with checkpointer/store passed at .compile() for memory.
routing_layer: application-layer. Routing is performed by an LLM node inside the application graph; there is no inference-engine-layer (Envoy/ext_proc) routing.
latency_overhead: One extra LLM round-trip per routing decision. Each supervisor-to-worker-to-supervisor cycle is two graph steps and at least one supervisor LLM call; a 4-specialist task realistically takes 6-10 steps. The supervisor's prompt must include all handoff-tool definitions, adding token overhead that grows with agent count. No upfront decomposition cost beyond the first supervisor call.
online_adaptation: static (fixed at deploy). Routing quality is governed by the supervisor prompt and tool descriptions; there is no bandit/RL or automatic fine-tuning from production logs. Improvement requires manual prompt/description edits.
adoption: open-source (with code) + production usage. langgraph-supervisor-py is MIT-licensed (latest 0.0.31, Nov 2025; ~1.6k stars). LangChain maintainers now recommend implementing the supervisor pattern directly via tools rather than this helper library for most use cases, positioning the library for legacy/convenience scenarios; the underlying pattern is widely deployed.
